presidents.name: William McKinley
presidents.summary: McKinley condemned lynching in his March 4, 1897 inaugural address but took no federal action against the wave of anti-Black violence and disfranchisement that ran through his presidency. When white supremacists overthrew Wilmington, North Carolina's elected government in November 1898 and killed Black residents, no federal aid was sent, and Black citizens organized to protest his public silence.
presidents.paragraph: McKinley used his inaugural to say that lynchings "must not be tolerated in a great and civilized country like the United States," and that courts, not mobs, should carry out the law. That's about as far as it went. The Miller Center's account says he refrained from acting against the anti-Black violence in the South that had "reached near epidemic proportions" in the century's last four years, and that his roughly thirty appointments of African Americans went mostly to diplomatic and records posts. On November 10, 1898, Alfred Moore Waddell led armed white men through Wilmington, North Carolina, driving out the elected Republican and Populist officials; North Carolina's own Department of Natural and Cultural Resources notes the dead are disputed and that many call it a massacre rather than a riot. No federal troops came. On October 3, 1899, Boston's Colored National League sent McKinley an open letter, now held by the Library of Congress, opening by naming his "incomprehensible silence" and saying Wilmington's self-government perished "for want of federal aid, which you would not and did not furnish."

presidents.name: Theodore Roosevelt
presidents.summary: Roosevelt hosted Booker T. Washington for dinner at the White House on October 16, 1901, the first time a President entertained a Black American there, and Southern press reaction was furious. Five years later, after a shooting in Brownsville, Texas, he discharged 167 Black soldiers of the 25th Infantry without honor and without a trial; Congress reversed the order in 1972.
presidents.paragraph: Two events frame Roosevelt's record. On October 16, 1901, weeks into his presidency, he had Booker T. Washington to dinner at the White House. The Washington Bee wrote three days later that Roosevelt was "The first President of the United States to entertain a colored man," and Southern papers reacted with fury. Then came Brownsville. On the night of August 13, 1906, shots in Brownsville, Texas killed one white civilian and wounded another. White townspeople blamed Black soldiers of the 25th Infantry at nearby Fort Brown, though the white officers said the men were in barracks. No court-martial was held, and a Texas court cleared them. Roosevelt discharged 167 men without honor anyway. In his December 19, 1906 message he said he ordered the discharge of nearly all of Companies B, C, and D "in the exercise of my constitutional power," citing a conspiracy of silence. They lost careers, pay, and pensions. He never apologized. In 1972 Congress reversed the dismissal order and made restitution.

presidents.name: William Howard Taft
presidents.summary: In his March 4, 1909 inaugural address Taft said the Executive must use careful discretion in appointing Black Americans and questioned whether appointing one to local office in a South with acute race feeling did more harm than good. In practice he appointed no new Black postmasters in the South and declined to reappoint incumbents as their terms lapsed, while making a handful of high-profile appointments in Washington.
presidents.paragraph: Taft laid out the policy in his own inaugural. He acknowledged the Reconstruction amendments, said the Fifteenth "attempted to secure the negro against any deprivation of the privilege to vote because he was a negro," and then said the Executive "must exercise a careful discretion not thereby to do it more harm than good." He doubted whether appointing a Black man to local office where race feeling was "so widespread and acute" was worth the increase in race feeling it would provoke, and told Black Americans to base their hope on "their own industry, self-restraint, thrift, and business success." The Postal Service's own history, citing historian Louis Harlan, records what that meant on the ground: Taft appointed no new Black postmasters in the South and refused to reappoint incumbents as their four-year terms expired, though the total number of Black postal employees kept growing. He also told the South it was "not the disposition or within the province of the Federal Government to interfere" with their domestic affairs.

presidents.name: Woodrow Wilson
presidents.summary: Beginning in 1913 Wilson's cabinet segregated federal workplaces, restrooms and cafeterias in departments including the Post Office and the Treasury, and Black federal employees were demoted and discharged. On February 18, 1915 he screened D.W. Griffith's The Birth of a Nation at the White House, and what he said about it is disputed.
presidents.paragraph: Wilson had courted Black voters in 1912 with talk of justice for all Americans. In office he let his cabinet segregate the federal workforce. The Miller Center records that he allowed members of his cabinet to introduce segregation into departments like the Post Office and Treasury, covering restrooms, cafeterias and offices, and that many Black federal workers were downgraded and discharged. USPS history notes Postmaster General Albert Burleson complaining about integrated conditions in the Railway Mail Service in April 1913, and a Civil Service Commission order of May 27, 1914 requiring applicant photographs, which let appointing officials screen out Black applicants. Research by Abhay Aneja and Guo Xu using 1907–1921 Official Registers found the Black-white civil service salary gap widened by about seven percentage points between 1913 and 1921. William Monroe Trotter confronted Wilson at the White House on November 12, 1914; Wilson declared himself offended and had him removed. On February 18, 1915, The Birth of a Nation was shown in the East Room.

disputes: The Birth of a Nation quotation. One tradition holds Wilson said the film was "like writing history with lightning" and that his only regret was that it was all so terribly true; the line has circulated in books and articles for decades. Against it: Mark E. Benbow's peer-reviewed 2010 study in the Journal of the Gilded Age and Progressive Era examines the quotation's provenance, and the Woodrow Wilson Presidential Library notes the line did not appear in print until roughly 22 years later and that Thomas Dixon, who arranged the screening, never mentioned it in his memoirs. Some accounts say Wilson paid little attention and left without comment. Recorded on both sides; not resolved here.

Wilson's own position on the screening: through secretary Joseph Tumulty he stated he was unaware of the film's character beforehand and had at no time expressed approbation of it; critics at the time treated the White House screening itself as an endorsement. Both recorded.
unverified: Whether Wilson signed any written executive order mandating segregation, as opposed to permitting cabinet-level department policies, was not verified from a fetched primary document.
The exact text and date of Wilson's reported 1918 proclamation against lynching and mob violence was not verified from a fetched primary source (referenced only in the Miller Center summary).

presidents.name: Warren G. Harding
presidents.summary: On April 12, 1921 Harding told a joint session of Congress it ought to wipe out the stain of barbaric lynching, and on October 26, 1921 he spoke about race at Birmingham's semicentennial. In the same Birmingham speech he endorsed political and economic rights for Black Americans while rejecting social equality and asserting an inescapable racial difference.
presidents.paragraph: Harding put lynching in a message to Congress six weeks into his term. On April 12, 1921 he told a joint session that "Congress ought to wipe the stain of barbaric lynching from the banners of a free and orderly, representative democracy," and floated a commission "embracing representatives of both races, to study and report on the entire subject." That October 26 he spoke at Birmingham's fiftieth-anniversary celebration and said the World War had brought full recognition that "the race problem is national rather than merely sectional." He wanted Black voters to stop being a single bloc and to vote Democratic if they preferred Democratic policy. But he also drew a hard line: men of both races, he said, should stand "uncompromisingly against every suggestion of social equality," which he framed as a fundamental and inescapable difference rather than a matter of rights. The Dyer anti-lynching bill passed the House on January 26, 1922 with his support and died to a Senate filibuster.

presidents.name: Calvin Coolidge
presidents.summary: In his first annual message on December 6, 1923 Coolidge said Black Americans' rights under the Constitution were as sacred as any other citizen's and urged Congress to use all its powers against lynching, and he recommended about half a million dollars for medical education at Howard University. He did not campaign for the Dyer anti-lynching bill, which Southern Democrats filibustered to death in the Senate.
presidents.paragraph: Coolidge said the words. In his first annual message on December 6, 1923 he noted the roughly 12 million colored people in the population, said that "under our Constitution their rights are just as sacred as those of any other citizen," and told Congress it "ought to exercise all its powers of prevention and punishment against the hideous crime of lynching." The same message recommended about half a million dollars for medical courses at Howard University. He was cooler on the two-race commission Harding had floated, treating these mostly as local matters. The Coolidge Presidential Library's own account says he declined to actively campaign for the Dyer bill, worried it would jeopardize priorities like tax reduction; the bill, which had cleared the House 230–119 on January 26, 1922, died to filibuster. On August 9, 1924 he wrote Charles F. Gardner that "a colored man is precisely as much entitled to submit his candidacy in a party primary, as is any other citizen." He spoke at Howard University's commencement on June 6, 1924.

callouts.text: Coolidge did not actively campaign for the Dyer anti-lynching bill, per the Coolidge Presidential Library, fearing it would jeopardize other priorities; the bill died to a Senate filibuster after passing the House 230–119.

sources.label: Forbes Library, Calvin Coolidge Presidential Library & Museum, "Coolidge and Civil Rights"
sources.quote: he ultimately declined to actively campaign for the bill's passage, fearing it would jeopardize other legislative priorities

sources.label: Megan Ming Francis, Civil Rights and the Making of the Modern American State (Cambridge Univ. Press, 2014)
sources.quote: the machinery of the United States Senate is antiquated to the point that millions of people may suffer injustice and death on account of it

sources.quote: The House approved the measure with a two-thirds majority (230-119).

disputes: Extent of desegregation under Coolidge: the Coolidge Presidential Library states segregation was "practically ended" in several departments by 1929 while noting cafeteria and restroom segregation persisted in some facilities. Recorded as stated, with the qualification intact.

Coolidge and the Dyer bill: his December 1923 message urged congressional action against lynching, while the Coolidge Presidential Library records that he declined to actively campaign for the bill. Both recorded.
unverified: The precise date and mechanics of the Senate filibuster that killed the Dyer bill (commonly given as December 1922) were not confirmed from a fetched Congressional Record or senate.gov page.
Whether Coolidge took any specific administrative action to desegregate federal departments, as distinct from segregation lapsing, was not verified from a primary source.
